summary:
## Account Setup & Configuration

- **Add Accounts**: Go to `File` > `Add Account` to add your first or subsequent email accounts. The automatic setup is recommended over the manual process.
- **Dark Mode**: To change your theme, navigate to `File` > `Office Account` > `Office Theme` and select `Dark Gray` or `Black`. This can reduce eye strain.

## Navigating Outlook

Outlook's interface consists of five key areas: Tabs, Folder Pane, Email List, Reading Pane, and the main Navigation Bar. 

> [!TIP]
> Use keyboard shortcuts to quickly switch between Outlook's functions:
> * **Mail**: `Ctrl + 1`
> * **Calendar**: `Ctrl + 2`
> * **Contacts**: `Ctrl + 3`
> * **Tasks**: `Ctrl + 4`

## Email Management

- **Composing**: Use `Ctrl + N` to create a new email. You can set **High Importance** with the red exclamation mark and attach files via the `Attach File` button or by **drag-and-drop**.
- **Responding to Invites**: Always respond to meeting invites by choosing `Accept`, `Tentative`, `Decline`, or `Propose New Time`. Avoid declining without sending a response.
- **Organizing the Inbox**: 
  - **Sorting**: Change the sort order from the default 'By Date' to 'From', 'Attachment', etc.
  - **Flags**: Left-click the flag icon on an email to set a quick follow-up reminder for today. Right-click for more options like custom dates.
  - **Folders**: Right-click on your inbox to create `New Folder`s for organizing emails by project or topic.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> For a cleaner inbox, go to the `View` tab and check **Show as Conversations**. This groups all replies in an email chain into a single, expandable line item.

## Search

Use the search bar at the top to find emails. You can perform a general search or use specific operators for more precision, such as:
- `from:John Doe`
- `hasattachment:yes`

## Calendar

- **Views**: Easily switch your calendar view between `Day`, `Work Week`, `Week`, and `Month` from the top ribbon.
- **Appointments vs. Meetings**: An **Appointment** is a time block for yourself. A **Meeting** includes other attendees.
- **Categorization**: Use `Categorize` on a meeting invitation to assign colors. This helps you quickly identify different types of events at a glance. You can customize category names and colors under `All Categories`.

## Contacts & Tasks

- **Adding Contacts**: Quickly add a sender to your contacts by **right-clicking their name** in an email and selecting `Add to Outlook Contacts`.
- **Tasks View**: This section provides a consolidated list of all your reminders and flagged items from across your emails and meetings.
transcription:
## Introduction: Become an Outlook Power User

This is the only introduction you'll ever need to master Microsoft Outlook's key functionalities, which is by the way a lot more than just emails. So by the end of the video, you'll know more about Outlook than probably 90% of your colleagues or friends. I've been using Outlook for more than 10 years and can tell it's easier than you might think, but at the same time, there are so many hidden but super useful and convenient functionalities that very few even advanced users know, but every one including you can highly benefit from. So let's discover Outlook's Essentials and some Insider tips and start off with setting up Outlook.

## Setting Up and Adding Email Accounts

In most cases, you will already have an active Outlook account and can start working with it right away. But in case you would like to connect your account to your Outlook desktop app for the first time, or in case you would like to add a second or a third account to your Outlook app, you need to open the desktop app on your computer. 

To add a second or third email account to Outlook, you need to go to File and Add Account. This will open another window that guides you through the process. In case it's your first account you're adding, this window will pop up right after having opened the Outlook app in the first place. Now you just need the respective email address and let Outlook automatically set up your account. I recommend not choosing the manual setup since this is a lot more complex, technical, and tedious. 

During the process, you might be required to enter your password if it's the first time you're setting up this account, and I would recommend remembering the credentials so you don't have to type them in every time you open Outlook. Finally, you are asked if you would like to add another account. If not, you can just finish and click done and potentially add another account anytime in the future.

## Pro Tip: Enabling Dark Mode

To finish your setup, I have a little bonus tip that lets you come across like a real power user right from the beginning. If you're not yet using the dark Microsoft Office theme, you can change this by going to File, down to Office Account, and to Office Theme. By choosing the dark gray or black theme, your Outlook and all other Office apps will change their look, which makes it easier to read, especially in the morning and evening hours when your surroundings are a bit darker than your screen.

## Navigating the Outlook Interface

Once you have set up your account, you will see the default Outlook interface with five main areas. At the top, you have different tabs that help you to manage your emails or organize and customize your inbox. We are going to cover the essential tabs being the Home, Folder, and View tab later on. 

The second key area is the inbox view on the left-hand side, which shows different folders of the account you're currently using. Next to this, you can see the list of emails in your inbox sorted by date, as well as the biggest area, the Reading Pane, that shows the email that you have selected from your list. 

Finally, there is the fifth main area, which is the navigation bar at the very left or at the bottom of Outlook. If you currently have it on the left but would like to move it back to the bottom or vice versa, just go to File, Options, Advanced, and check or uncheck the box saying 'Show apps in Outlook' underneath the very top section, Outlook Panes. 

The navigation bar is super helpful to quickly jump between Outlook's key functionalities, which are emails, the calendar, your contacts, and tasks. You can either just click on the respective icon or jump from Outlook to the calendar by clicking Control + 2, to the contact list by clicking Control + 3, and to the to-dos with Control + 4, and back to emails with Control + 1.

## Sending, Receiving, and Replying to Emails

Starting with emails, the most important feature are obviously sending and receiving emails. As long as you are connected with the internet and have set up your account properly, you should automatically be receiving emails, since Outlook regularly checks in the background if something has arrived for you. In case you would like to check manually, you can either just press F9 or go to the Send and Receive tab and click Send and Receive All Folders. 

In case you receive an email with a meeting invite, you should always send an answer to the sender. You do that by using the four buttons at the top right to either accept the meeting, accept it tentatively, decline it, or suggest an alternative timing. You always have the option to edit and add a response to the sender, just send your response without text, or just accept tentatively, accept, or decline without sending a response. I would never recommend doing the latter since this leaves a sender in the dark as to whether you're participating or not. 

To send an email you just need to click on New Email, the very first icon on the top left under the Home tab, or use the shortcut Control + N. Then a new window pops up. First, you can choose from which email account you would like to send the email to, in case you have set up several ones in your Outlook app. And second, you can insert one or more recipients and people in CC, which means those are being copied onto the email but are not directly addressed. When adding several people, you separate the email addresses with a semicolon. Having entered the subject of the email and the message below, you can click Send. In case you would like to increase the importance of your email and make it pop in the recipient inbox, you can set it to high importance by clicking on the red exclamation mark. 

To attach one or several files to your email, you need to click on Attach File in the middle of the message tab. It will show you a list of your recently used files, but most commonly you will need to browse your computer and use the file explorer to choose the file you want to send. Alternatively, you can also just drag and drop it from its location to your email.

## Organizing with Sorting & Flags

Going back to your email inbox, you might have noticed that all your emails are sorted by date. It is as it says on top right of your messages preview bar. To get a better overview, you can fold in or out your emails by day or week, but you can also use a different sorting method by clicking on the button that currently says 'By Date'. For example, you could choose to sort the emails by sender, attachment, or flag. Flags are a way to add reminders to your individual emails. So whenever you hover above an email in the preview pane, a small flag will appear on the right side. By left clicking, a follow-up reminder with today as a due date will be set. By right clicking on the flag, you will be able to choose the due date or customize the flag: its purpose, start and end date, as well as when you will receive a reminder.

## Customizing Your Inbox View and Layout

You might have seen already that the preview pane has two tabs or views itself being 'Focused' and 'Other'. In the 'Focused' view, you will see all of your important emails from known contacts or that have exchanged emails in the past already. Whilst in the 'Other' tab, you will receive emails from less known or almost spammy contacts. But if you would like to get rid of those two tabs, you can go to the overall View tab and then uncheck 'Show Focused Inbox'. Instead of an 'Focused' and 'Other', you will now have the 'All' and the 'Unread' view of your inbox. 

Staying on the View tab for a moment, you can also change the message preview, so the length of each message that will be shown in the preview pane. The default is one line, but you can change it to two or three or turn it off. This might be useful if you also want to change the layout of some of the other panes, which you can also do under the View tab, under Layout. First, you can decide if you want to minimize the folder pane or keep it open. Second, you can choose to show the reading pane at the right as per default, at the bottom, or turn it off completely. And third, you can add other useful bars to the right-hand side of Outlook, namely the calendar, contacts, or your tasks. 

One final, very useful setting that I love is to make your emails and Outlook appear as conversations, which can be done by checking the box that says 'Show as Conversations'. I recommend choosing 'All Inboxes' so all emails from the same email chain will be shown as one line item that you can unfold to view all emails from the chain. I believe this helps to keep an overview and have all emails on the same topic at one place instead of scrolling up or down to find the related ones you're looking for.

## Managing Folders and Searching Emails

What's also important is to know how to handle folders in Outlook. There are quite a few on the left side in the default Outlook setup, for example the Inbox, Drafts, or Sent Items, but you can also create additional folders to organize your emails by topic, project, or sender. Just do a right click on the Inbox and choose New Folder that you can name. Now you can pull individual emails into that folder and sort them via drag and drop, or by right clicking on the overarching folder and choosing to sort the subfolders from A to Z. 

In case you're not sure anymore where to find an email, you can use the search bar on top. Very basic, you can just type in anything related to the email, such as title or content, or you can use specific prompts such as 'from:' and then mention a specific sender, or 'has attachment: yes' or 'no'.

## A Quick Note from the Creator

Taking a quick break here. Let me know in the comments if you liked this tutorial so far and if you would like to see part two on my channel. Also, don't forget to subscribe to my newsletter by the link in the description to receive regular quick tips and advice on Microsoft tools and how to become more productive at work.

## Mastering the Outlook Calendar

The calendar is Outlook's second essential functionality that has four main areas. On top, very similar tabs to the inbox view. On the top left is a two or more month mini calendar overview. Below, your own calendars from the email accounts you have added to Outlook, as well as the ones of your team in case you work in an organization that has enabled this view. And on the right, your calendar overview. By default, usually a whole week is shown, but you can change this by choosing a different time frame at the top—either to show a single day, a work week only, or an entire month. Usually, I prefer to show a work week so I know at one glance what's going on in that week. To set up a meeting, you can either click on the button for New Appointment or New Meeting on the top left. An appointment does not include any other participants, whilst a new meeting has line items for required and optional participants, but in case you click on a new appointment, you can always add others by clicking on the button to invite attendees. Once you have entered the title, participants, and location, and set the start and end time, you send the invite by clicking 'Save and Close.' Now the invite will appear in your calendar overview and in the inbox of the attendees you have added. A very useful feature I'm using in particular to organize my calendar is Outlook's ability to categorize meetings or emails. I prefer to have a nice overview that helps me spot meetings with different importance or participants at one glance. So you can set different categories when having an invite open by clicking on 'Categorize.' Outlook's default categories look a bit different, but you can tailor them to your needs by clicking on 'All Categories'.

## Managing Outlook Contacts

Your Outlook contact list might be pre-filled by your company's contacts, so your colleagues, or it's empty and you can add contacts from emails or from scratch. To add a contact from an email, you need to open an email where the person is shown in the To, CC, or BCC line. Then right-click on the name of the person and select 'Add to Outlook Contacts.' You might want to add a few additional details and click 'Save and Close.' To add a contact from scratch, you can click on 'New Contact' in the Contacts tab, fill the contact details, and save and close again.

## Using the Tasks View

And finally, there is the Tasks view in Outlook that shows an overview of your tasks, reminders, and other flags that you have set based on your emails or meetings. Like the email preview pane, there is a task preview pane that lists all of your tasks, and once you select one, the respective email or meeting that you have tagged or flagged will be shown on the right-hand side.

## Conclusion and What's Next

In the beginning, I mentioned that by watching this video, you will know more about Outlook than 90% of your colleagues, but there's even more tips and tricks that will get you to 99%. So check out this video where I'll share some of the most useful Outlook productivity tips for you to make your life even more easier and efficient.
